predecessors.name: Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth
predecessors.text: South Prussia of 1793: the Poznań, Kalisz and Gniezno voivodeships of Greater Poland (south of the Netze District), the lands of Sieradz and Łęczyca, the Kuyavian voivodeship of Brześć and Dobrzyń…

successors.name: Duchy of Warsaw
successors.text: South Prussia of 1795 with Warsaw, without Dobrzyń Land northeast of the Vistula (New East Prussia)

ledger.x: 25 September 1793: the Second Partition gives Prussia South Prussia.
1795: 'After the Third Partition, the lands of Dobrzyń and Płock northeast of the Vistula river were transferred to New East Prussia'.
1806: the Greater Poland Uprising ('took place in 1806', no date on the page) after Napoleon's victory in the War of the Fourth Coalition; South Prussia is contested until the Treaties of Tilsit.
9 July 1807: the Treaties of Tilsit end the contest; South Prussia goes to the Duchy of Warsaw, a French client state (see the next event).

9 July 1807: 'the territory of South Prussia became part of the Duchy of Warsaw, a French client state, according to the 1807 Treaties of Tilsit' (Poznań, Kalisz, Gniezno, Sieradz, Łęczyca, Brześć Kujawski, Płock, Rawa and Masovian voivodeships).
9 July 1807: South Prussia ends; after 1815 it was 'divided between the Prussian Grand Duchy of Posen and Congress Poland'.

wars.name: Second Partition of Poland
wars.outcome: After the Polish-Russian War of 1792 Prussia took 58,000 km2 and Russia 250,000 km2; the Commonwealth 'lost about 307,000 km2, being reduced to 215,000 km2'.

wars.name: Greater Poland Uprising
wars.outcome: Napoleon's victory and the uprising of 1806 ended Prussian rule; the Treaties of Tilsit (9 July 1807) gave South Prussia to the Duchy of Warsaw.

certainty.note: Partition treaty lines (1793, 1795) and river borders (the Pilica, the Netze District line); the pages list voivodeships, not survey lines, so the sharp level rests on the treaties and the drawn polygons are approximate.
